distractorExplanations.a: Vitamin C is water-soluble and not stored long-term in adipose tissue; excess is excreted in urine rather than accumulating with dietary fat.
distractorExplanations.b: Thiamin (B1) is a water-soluble B vitamin used in decarboxylation reactions; it is not one of the fat-soluble A/D/E/K group.
distractorExplanations.d: Folate (B9) is water-soluble; fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, and K, which need bile and dietary fat for absorption.

rd-exam-readiness-check-principles-021.explanation: Fat provides 9 kcal per gram, so 50 g fat yields 450 kcal. On a 2000 kcal diet that is 450 ÷ 2000 = 0.225, about 23% of energy from fat — close to typical AMDR fat ranges, not 10% or 50%.

distractorExplanations.b: 10% of 2000 kcal is 200 kcal, which would be only about 22 g fat at 9 kcal/g; 50 g fat is more than twice that.
distractorExplanations.c: 50% of 2000 kcal is 1000 kcal, or about 111 g fat; 50 g fat is roughly a quarter of energy, not half.
distractorExplanations.d: Fat is energy-dense at 9 kcal/g, so 50 g cannot contribute 0% of calories on a mixed diet.
Preferred dessert choice is a food preference, not an AND/ASPEN malnutrition characteristic; diagnosis needs at least two of intake, weight, muscle/fat, fluid, or function findings.

options.b: Laissez-faire with no direction or follow-up
options.d: Transactional leadership limited to rewards and punishments

distractorExplanations.a: Autocratic leaders decide alone and issue orders; they do not invite staff into the decision before choosing a course.
distractorExplanations.b: Laissez-faire withdraws guidance; participative/democratic solicits employee input and then the leader still decides.
distractorExplanations.d: Transactional leadership exchanges rewards or sanctions for performance; it is not the same as inviting staff into decisions.

distractorExplanations.b: Protein, dairy, sodium, and alcohol are nutrient groups, not the Deming/Shewhart quality-improvement cycle letters.
distractorExplanations.d: Policy-discipline-suspend-arrest is a punitive HR sequence, not Plan-Do-Study-Act used in QI.

rd-exam-readiness-check-foodservice-017.explanation: FDA Food Code hot-holding for TCS/PHF foods is 135°F (57°C) or above so the product stays out of the temperature danger zone during service. Cold-hold is a separate 41°F rule; room temperature is not a hold method.

distractorExplanations.b: 41°F or below is the cold-holding limit for TCS foods, not a hot-line target; putting hot food at 41°F is cooling, not hot holding.
distractorExplanations.c: Room temperature sits in the danger zone (~41–135°F) where pathogens multiply; it is not an approved hot-hold.
distractorExplanations.d: A single unverified 100°F reading is still in the danger zone and does not meet the 135°F hot-hold critical limit.

rd-exam-readiness-check-foodservice-021.explanation: Two-stage cooling requires cooked TCS food to drop from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then from 70°F to 41°F within 4 more hours (6 hours total). The first-stage 2-hour limit is what this item tests.

distractorExplanations.b: Eight hours at room temperature leaves food in the danger zone far beyond the 2-hour first-stage cooling limit.
distractorExplanations.c: A warm oven holds heat; it cannot meet the 135→70°F in 2 hours cooling critical limit.
distractorExplanations.d: Overnight counter cooling violates both stages of the Food Code cooling rule and is a classic outbreak setup.

rd-exam-readiness-check-foodservice-022.explanation: Leftovers that were cooked, cooled, then reheated for hot holding must reach 165°F (74°C) for 15 seconds. That leftover-reheat rule is separate from poultry cook CCPs (165°F instantaneous in current Food Code) and from 135°F hot-hold of commercially processed intact RTE items.

distractorExplanations.c: 41°F is refrigeration/cold-hold, not a reheat endpoint; leftovers for the steam table must be reheated to 165°F, not chilled.
distractorExplanations.d: Visible steam is not a validated critical limit; leftover reheat for hot holding is measured at 165°F for 15 seconds with a thermometer.

rd-exam-readiness-check-foodservice-030.explanation: Blast chillers pull cooked product through the temperature danger zone quickly so cook-chill operations can meet two-stage cooling limits before refrigerated storage. They are cooling equipment, not hot-hold or thaw tools.

distractorExplanations.a: Hot holding at 135°F uses steam tables or hot cabinets; a blast chiller is designed to drop temperature, not maintain hot-hold.
distractorExplanations.c: Thawing at room temperature is unsafe; blast chillers cool cooked food, they are not a thaw method.
distractorExplanations.d: Long-term 41°F storage is a refrigerator or walk-in job after blast chilling is finished, not the blast chiller’s purpose.
